source.name: usp_UpdateInventory

result.generatedDdl:
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE dbo.usp_UpdateInventory(
    p_ProductID INT,
    p_NewQuantity INT
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    -- SET NOCOUNT ON equivalent: PostgreSQL doesn't send row counts by default in procedures
    
    UPDATE dbo.Products p
    SET StockQuantity = p_NewQuantity
    WHERE p.ProductID = p_ProductID
    FOR UPDATE; -- Equivalent to UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK for row-level locking
    
END;
$$;
assumptions: The schema 'dbo' exists in PostgreSQL or will be created
The Products table exists with columns ProductID and StockQuantity
INT type mapping is appropriate for both ProductID and NewQuantity
Row-level locking behavior with FOR UPDATE is acceptable replacement for WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK)
Parameter naming convention changed from @ParamName to p_ParamName to follow PostgreSQL best practices
SET NOCOUNT ON is not needed as PostgreSQL procedures don't return row counts by default

reviewFlags.reason: SQL Server's WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) hint provides update lock during SELECT. PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE in UPDATE statement locks rows being updated. The locking semantics differ: SQL Server hint prevents other transactions from reading locked rows with certain isolation levels, while PostgreSQL's default behavior allows reads. Consider if additional locking strategy or isolation level changes are needed.
PostgreSQL UPDATE syntax differs from SQL Server. The alias 'p' is used differently. Verify the UPDATE statement works correctly with the target PostgreSQL version and table structure.

Parameters renamed from @ProductID to p_ProductID to avoid confusion with column names in WHERE clause. Ensure calling applications are updated to match new parameter names if using named parameter syntax.

compatibilityNotes.description: SQL Server's WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) hint and PostgreSQL's row locking have different semantics. SQL Server's UPDLOCK prevents other transactions from acquiring shared locks, while PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE only blocks conflicting locks. The default isolation levels also differ (READ COMMITTED in both, but implementation varies).

SQL Server stored procedures run in implicit transactions by default. PostgreSQL procedures can control transactions explicitly. This procedure will run within the caller's transaction context if one exists, or in autocommit mode otherwise.
SQL Server's SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses 'rows affected' messages. PostgreSQL procedures don't return row counts to clients by default, so this is implicitly handled.
The original procedure has no explicit error handling. PostgreSQL will raise exceptions on errors by default. Consider adding EXCEPTION blocks if specific error handling is needed.
